Expo ships breaking changes every SDK release. APIs you remember are likely renamed, moved, or removed. Before writing any code that touches an Expo, EAS, or React Native API:

This is an Expo/React Native mobile application. Prioritize mobile-first patterns, performance, and cross-platform compatibility.

## Expo has changed — do not trust your training data

Expo ships breaking changes every SDK release. APIs you remember are likely renamed, moved, or removed. Before writing any code that touches an Expo, EAS, or React Native API:

1. Read the major version of the `expo` package in `package.json`.
2. Fetch the matching versioned docs: `https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v<major>.0.0/`
3. For anything else, fetch https://docs.expo.dev/llms.txt — an index of all Expo docs with corrections to common LLM misconceptions. Follow its links to the specific page you need; never answer from memory.

## Commands

Use `bunx` instead of `npx` if the project uses bun (`bun.lock` present).

```bash
npx expo install <package>  # ALWAYS use instead of npm/yarn/pnpm/bun add — resolves SDK-compatible versions
npx expo start              # start the dev server
npx expo lint               # lint
npx tsc --noEmit            # typecheck
npx expo-doctor             # diagnose dependency and config issues
npx expo install --fix      # fix incompatible package versions
```

Run lint and typecheck before declaring any task done.

## Navigation & Routing

- Use **Expo Router** for all navigation. Routes live in `src/app/` — every file there is a screen, `_layout.tsx` files define navigators. Keep non-route code (components, hooks, utils) outside `src/app/`.
- Import `Link`, `router`, and `useLocalSearchParams` from `expo-router`.
- Docs: https://docs.expo.dev/router/introduction.md

## Building with EAS

Use EAS to build, sign, and submit the app in the cloud (`eas build`, `eas submit`) and to ship over-the-air updates (`eas update`) — no local Xcode or Android Studio required. Run EAS CLI as `bunx eas-cli <command>` in Bun projects, or `npx eas-cli@latest <command>` otherwise; substitute that for bare `eas` in docs examples.
Docs: https://docs.expo.dev/eas/index.md

## Rules

- If `ios/` and `android/` directories do not exist, they are generated (Continuous Native Generation). Never create or edit them by hand — configure native behavior in `app.json` and config plugins.
- Expo Go only includes its bundled native modules. After adding a library with native code, the app needs a development build: `npx expo run:ios|android` locally, or `eas build --profile development`.
- Prefer recommended Expo modules over third-party libraries, and check your available skills before adding dependencies. Docs: https://docs.expo.dev/versions/latest/index.md

The Expo SDK is a collection of packages that provide access to device and system functionality such as camera, contacts, location, sensors, haptics, and more. Each package targets a specific feature and can be used independently. All packages work in any React Native app with the `expo` package installed.

You can install any Expo SDK package using the [`npx expo install`](https://docs.expo.dev/more/expo-cli.md#install) command. For example, three different packages are installed using the following command:

```sh
npx expo install expo-camera expo-contacts expo-sensors
```

After installing one or more packages, you can import them into your JavaScript code:

```ts
import { CameraView } from 'expo-camera';
import { Contact } from 'expo-contacts';
import { Gyroscope } from 'expo-sensors';
```

This allows you to write [`Contact.getAll()`](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v57.0.0/sdk/contacts.md#getalloptions) and read the contacts from the device, read the gyroscope sensor to detect device movement, or start the phone's camera and take photos.

## All Expo SDK packages work in any React Native app

Expo apps are React Native apps, so all Expo SDK packages work in any React Native app with the `expo` package installed and configured. The easiest way to create a React Native app with support for Expo SDK packages is to use `create-expo-app`. However, you can also add Expo SDK support to an existing React Native app with the `npx install-expo-modules` command.

```sh
# Create a project named my-app
npx create-expo-app my-app --template bare-minimum
```

[Install Expo SDK packages in existing React Native apps](https://docs.expo.dev/bare/installing-expo-modules.md) — Learn more about configuring projects created with npx @react-native-community/cli@latest init to Expo SDK packages. — npx @react-native-community/cli@latest init

[Use libraries](https://docs.expo.dev/workflow/using-libraries.md) — Learn how to install Expo SDK packages in your project.

## Using pre-release versions

New Expo SDK versions are released three times each year. Between these releases, we publish pre-release versions of the `expo` package and all of the Expo SDK packages. Pre-releases are not considered stable and should only be used if you are comfortable with the risk of encountering bugs or other issues.

### Canary releases

Canary releases represent a snapshot of the state of the `main` branch at the time they are published. Canary package versions include `-canary` in the name, along with the date and commit hash, such as `57.0.0-canary-20260526-13e89ca`. To install the latest canary release:

```sh
# Install the alpha version of expo and its related packages
npm install expo@canary && npx expo install --fix
```

You can often use pre-release versions of individual packages with stable releases of the Expo SDK. There may occasionally be incompatibilities or other issues that arise in canary-quality releases. You may want to [silence dependency validation warnings](https://docs.expo.dev/more/expo-cli.md#configuring-dependency-validation) if you opt in to the canary package and once you have verified that it works well for your use cases.

### Beta releases

Before each Expo SDK release, we publish beta versions of the `expo` package and all of the Expo SDK packages. Beta releases are considered much more stable than canary releases, and we encourage developers to try them out on their apps and share their feedback. Beta releases use the `beta` tag on npm and follow the instructions in the related [changelog](https://expo.dev/changelog) post.

## Each Expo SDK version depends on a React Native version

| Expo SDK version | React Native version | React version | React Native Web version | React Native TV version | Minimum Node.js version |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 57.0.0 | 0.86 | 19.2.3 | 0.21.0 | 0.86-stable | 22.13.x |
| 56.0.0 | 0.85 | 19.2.3 | 0.21.0 | 0.85-stable | 20.19.x |
| 55.0.0 | 0.83 | 19.2.0 | 0.21.0 | 0.83-stable | 20.19.x |
| 54.0.0 | 0.81 | 19.1.0 | 0.21.0 | 0.81-stable | 20.19.x |

### Additional information

#### Expo SDK policy for tracking React Native releases

-   Each Expo SDK release targets a single React Native version. This is typically the latest stable version at the time of the release.
-   React Native currently has six releases per year and aims for every release to include no breaking changes.
-   Expo SDK releases aim to follow this cadence.
-   Pre-release versions of the upcoming Expo SDK will include support for the latest version of React Native quickly, usually the same day it is released. A member of the Expo SDK team works on the React Native releases team for each release, and is responsible for continuously updating the React Native version in the Expo repository, verifying compatibility, and reporting regressions back to the React Native team.

#### What if I need a change from the latest React Native version and it's not yet in an Expo SDK release?

Expo engineers on the React Native releases team ensure that any urgent fixes are included in the React Native version used by the latest Expo SDK. If your specific fix won't be cherrypicked into an existing release, perhaps because it is not considered critical or because it involves a breaking change, then you have two options:

1.  Use [`patch-package`](https://github.com/ds300/patch-package) to pull in the fix.
2.  Use a [pre-release version of the Expo SDK](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v57.0.0.md#using-pre-release-versions).

#### Can I use an older version of React Native with the latest Expo SDK?

Packages in the Expo SDK are intended to support the target React Native version for that SDK. Typically, they will not support older versions of React Native, but they may. When a new version of React Native is released, the latest versions of the Expo SDK packages are typically updated to support it. However, this may take weeks or more, depending on the extent of the changes in the release.

## Support for Android and iOS versions

Each version of Expo SDK supports a minimum OS version of Android and iOS. For Android, the `compileSdkVersion` is defined which tells the [Gradle](https://developer.android.com/studio/build) which Android SDK version to use to compile the app. This also means that you can use the Android API features included in that SDK version and from the previous versions. For iOS, the [Xcode](https://developer.apple.com/news/upcoming-requirements/) tells the minimum Xcode SDK version to use to compile the app.

| Expo SDK version | Android version | `compileSdkVersion` | `targetSdkVersion` | iOS version | Xcode version |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 57.0.0 | 7+ | 36 | 36 | 16.4+ | 26.4+ |
| 56.0.0 | 7+ | 36 | 36 | 16.4+ | 26.4+ |
| 55.0.0 | 7+ | 36 | 36 | 15.1+ | 26.2+ |
| 54.0.0 | 7+ | 36 | 36 | 15.1+ | 16.1+ |

When deciding whether to upgrade your Expo SDK version, consider both Expo's SDK version and app store submission requirements, as described in the above table. Google Play Store and Apple App Store periodically increase their minimum required OS versions and API levels, which are required for new app submissions. Expo has no control over the app store requirements, and you should check [Google](https://developer.android.com/studio/build) and [Apple](https://developer.apple.com/news/upcoming-requirements/) for the current store submission requirements.

- `react-native-worklets` no encuentra `fbjniConfig.cmake`.
- `react-native-screens` no encuentra `ReactAndroidConfig.cmake`.

Ambos son paquetes que Gradle debería proporcionar mediante **Prefab**. Eso apunta a que sus artefactos no están disponibles en la configuración de Android generada o en la resolución de dependencias; no indica un error en el código C++ de la app.

Las versiones declaradas en `apps/mobile/package.json` sí coinciden a grandes rasgos: Expo SDK 57 usa React Native 0.86, y el proyecto declara RN 0.86.3. La advertencia sobre la versión XML del SDK y los avisos de Kotlin no son la causa que detiene esta compilación.

Como `android/` es un proyecto generado por Expo, el siguiente paso razonable es regenerarlo limpiamente y volver a compilar:

```powershell
npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo prebuild --platform android --clean
npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo run:android
```

`--clean` vuelve a generar el proyecto nativo; si hay cambios manuales dentro de `apps/mobile/android`, conviene respaldarlos antes. Si el error persiste, comparte la salida de `expo-doctor` y el nuevo primer error de Gradle: eso permitirá distinguir entre un problema de generación del proyecto y uno de resolución de Prefab.

content.text:
Title: [expo-updates][Android] Honor rootProject.ext.ndkVersion
URL: https://github.com/expo/expo/pull/45759
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
`packages/expo-updates/android/build.gradle` does not declare an `ndkVersion`, so AGP falls back to its own preferred version (currently `27.0.12077973`). When a host project sets `rootProject.ext.ndkVersion` to anything else (e.g. RN 0.83 sets `27.1.12297006` via `react-native/gradle/libs.versions.toml`), `expo-updates`'s `externalNativeBuild` path triggers `[CXX1104]`:
...
Other modules in this repo (e.g. `packages/expo-modules-core/android/build.gradle`) already gate `ndkVersion` on `rootProject.hasProperty("ndkVersion")` and pick it up from the host project, which is what makes the build succeed when the host project (or `expo-root-project`) sets a non-default NDK. `expo-updates` was missing this block.
...
Add the same `if (rootProject.hasProperty("ndkVersion")) { ndkVersion rootProject.ext.ndkVersion }` block to `packages/expo-updates/android/build.gradle`, matching the canonical pattern in `expo-modules-core`. No other change.
...
> 
> 
> **Outcome: pass**
> 
> 
> @brentvatne — Reproduced, and the change fixes it. In a Gradle build on SDK 57, `:expo-updates` resolves NDK `27.0.12077973`, AGP 8.12's default, while the host project uses `27.1.12297006`. The build then fails with the exact `[CXX1104]` message from the report. With the 4 lines here, `:expo-updates` resolves `27.1.12297006` and the native build succeeds.
> 
> @xxih — the diagnosis and the `build.gradle` change are correct, and that hunk still merges. One thing is needed from you: a rebase. The `CHANGELOG.md` entry conflicts with `main`. Move it into the current `Unpublished` section. Keep the `pnpm patch` workaround until a release ships.
> 
> For a maintainer: the code change is right, so it can merge after the rebase. One call is yours. `expo-updates` is not the only module with this gap. `expo-sqlite` and `expo-widgets` also compile CMake code and also set no `ndkVersion`. Take this pull request, which copies the pattern already in `expo-modules-core`. Then fix the other two. Or set `ndkVersion` once in `applyDefaultAndroidSdkVersions`, next to `compileSdk` and `minSdk`. I did not write it: it changes every Expo module.
> 
> Environment 
> 
> Hosted Linux sandbox. No simulator or emulator ran. This is a Gradle configuration bug, so every decisive artifact is build output, not a screenshot. No EAS build was used.
> 
> - App: `create-expo-app@latest`, SDK 57 — `expo@57.0.16`, `react-native@0.86.2`, `expo-updates@57.0.17`
> - `npx expo prebuild -p android`
> - JDK 17.0.20, Gradle 9.3.1, Android SDK command-line tools 13114758, platform `android-36`, build-tools `36.0.0`, CMake 3.22.1
> - From `react-native/gradle/libs.versions.toml`: `agp = "8.12.0"`, `ndkVersion = "27.1.12297006"`
> - Pull request revision read: `a2b03ef`
> 
> The report describes SDK 55 and React Native 0.83. I did not re-run that exact configuration. I used SDK 57, the release this fix would ship in. The mechanism does not depend on the version. It depends on the module reading `rootProject.ext.ndkVersion` or not.
> 
> I applied the pull request's 4 lines to `node_modules/expo-updates/android/build.gradle` for the "after" arm. That file and the one this pull request changes are the same in the region that matters. A `diff` against the checkout at `64b4544` shows three differences: the version strings (`56.0.17` in the repository, `57.0.17` on npm), the `abiFilters(*reactNativeArchitectures())` line added by #49299 and not yet published, and the 4 lines I applied. Neither file sets `ndkVersion`.
> 
> 
> 
> Measurement 1 — which NDK each module resolves 
> 
> A Gradle init script printed `android.ndkVersion` for every subproject after evaluation:
> 
> ```
> NDKPROBE root.ext.ndkVersion=27.1.12297006
> NDKPROBE :app android.ndkVersion=27.1.12297006
> NDKPROBE :expo-modules-core android.ndkVersion=27.1.12297006
> NDKPROBE :expo-updates android.ndkVersion=27.0.12077973
> NDKPROBE :expo android.ndkVersion=27.0.12077973
> NDKPROBE :expo-constants android.ndkVersion=27.0.12077973
> NDKPROBE :expo-eas-client android.ndkVersion=27.0.12077973
> NDKPROBE :expo-json-utils android.ndkVersion=27.0.12077973
> NDKPROBE :expo-log-box android.ndkVersion=27.0.12077973
> NDKPROBE :expo-manifests android.ndkVersion=27.0.12077973
> NDKPROBE :expo-structured-headers android.ndkVersion=27.0.12077973
> NDKPROBE :expo-updates-interface android.ndkVersion=27.0.12077973
> ```
> 
> `27.0.12077973` is AGP 8.12's default. Only `:app` and `:expo-modules-core` follow the host project. The other modules show the default too. They compile no native code, so the value never reaches an NDK lookup for them. `:expo-updates` is the one module that compiles CMake code and ignores the host value.
> 
> After the pull request's 4 lines, the same probe prints this, filtered to the two lines that changed:
> 
> ```
> NDKPROBE root.ext.ndkVersion=27.1.12297006
> NDKPROBE :expo-updates android.ndkVersion=27.1.12297006
> ```
> 
> 
> 
> Measurement 2 — the reported [CXX1104] failure, before and after 
> 
> Setup: only NDK `27.1.12297006` installed, and `ndk.dir` set in `android/local.properties`. This is the reporter's setup.
> 
> Before, `./gradlew :expo-updates:externalNativeBuildDebug`:
> 
> ```
> * What went wrong:
> A problem occurred evaluating project ':expo'.
> > Failed to apply plugin 'expo-autolinking'.
> > A problem occurred configuring project ':expo-updates'.
> > [CXX1104] NDK from ndk.dir at /home/user/sdk/ndk/27.1.12297006 had version [27.1.12297006] which disagrees with android.ndkVersion [27.0.12077973]
> 
> BUILD FAILED in 2s
> ```
> 
> That is the message in the pull request description, apart from the paths.
> 
> After the 4 lines, same command, same setup:
> 
> ```
> BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 8s
> ```
> 
> The run compiled the library. AGP wrote a new CMake hash directory, and `libexpo-updates.so` appeared under it for all four ABIs:
> 
> ```
> .cxx/Debug/5w1i6m51/{arm64-v8a,armeabi-v7a,x86,x86_64}
> build/intermediates/cxx/Debug/5w1i6m51/obj/arm64-v8a/libexpo-updates.so 547992 bytes
> ```
...
> 
> 
> 
> Cause 
> 
> `expo-module-gradle-plugin` applies `compileSdk` and `minSdk` from the root project, and nothing else. See `applyDefaultAndroidSdkVersions` and `applySDKVersions`. Neither sets `ndkVersion`.
> 
> The root project does hold the value. `ExpoRootProjectPlugin.defineDefaultProperties` reads `ndkVersion` from React Native's version catalog and stores it in `rootProject.ext`.
> 
> So each module that compiles native code must read it back itself. Two modules do: `expo-modules-core` and `expo-gl`. `expo-updates` does not, and it declares `externalNativeBuild { cmake { path "CMakeLists.txt" } }`.
> 
> One small difference from the reference pattern: `expo-modules-core` also gates `ndkPath`, and this pull request copies only the `ndkVersion` half.
> 
> 
>

Title: [expo-updates][Android] CMake build ignores reactNativeArchitectures and builds unused ABIs
URL: https://github.com/expo/expo/issues/49291
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
# [expo-updates][Android] CMake build ignores reactNativeArchitectures and builds unused ABIs
...
This is a source-level Android build issue in `expo-updates`; no application code is required. The current SDK 57 source and the published `expo-updates@57.0.17` tarball both reproduce the missing ABI filtering.
...
Create/pre ... a bare Expo SDK 57 Android ... that includes `expo-updates@57.0.17`.
...
_64
...
`expo-updates` should honor `reactNativeArchitectures=x86_64`, consistent with other Expo C++ modules, and configure/build CMake only for x86_64.
...
`expo-updates/android/build.gradle` declares `externalNativeBuild.cmake` but never applies `reactNativeArchitectures` as an ABI filter:

https://github.com/expo/expo/blob/sdk-57/packages/expo-updates/android/build.gradle#L89-L113

As a result, x86_64-only builds still configure/build the `expo-updates` native code for unused Android ABIs. This adds avoidable CMake/NDK work to emulator and CI builds.

Other Expo modules already handle the property. For example, `expo-modules-core`, `expo-gl`, and `expo-sqlite` define a `reactNativeArchitectures()` helper and pass it to `abiFilters`.
...
- `expo-updates@57.0.10`
- `expo-updates@57.0.11`
- `expo-updates@57.0.17` (latest at the time of filing)

A working local workaround is:

```gradle
defaultConfig {
  if (project.hasProperty("reactNativeArchitectures")) {
    ndk {
      abiFilters(*project.property("reactNativeArchitectures").split(","))
    }
  }
}
```

For consistency with other Expo modules, the upstream implementation could instead reuse their helper pattern:

```gradle
def reactNativeArchitectures() {
  def value = project.getProperties().get("reactNativeArchitectures")
  return value ? value.split(",") : ["armeabi-v7a", "x86", "x86_64", "arm64-v8a"]
}

// inside externalNativeBuild.cmake
abiFilters(*reactNativeArchitectures())
```

This is a build-performance issue rather than an APK correctness issue. Default production builds can continue building all configured ABIs; explicit single-ABI builds should not compile the others.

...

The Android Gradle plugin does not provide built-in support for artifacts that
include native libraries (for linking against) and header files. Because of
that, some manual additions to your build system are required. The following
is an example of what this can look like but by no means prescriptive.

android {

  // The Android Gradle Plugin 3.* does not allow hooking into existing
  // configurations like `implementation`.
  configurations {
    extractHeaders
    extractJNI
  }

  dependencies {
    implementation 'com.facebook.fbjni:fbjni:0.0.1'
    // If headers are required.
    extractHeaders 'com.facebook.fbjni:fbjni:0.0.1:headers'
    // If the `.so` files are required for linking.
    extractJNI 'com.facebook.fbjni:fbjni:0.0.1'
  }
}

and JNI shared libraries will be extracted under the build directory.

Now, in your CMake setup, you can refer to the `fbjni` package. The header files (e.g. `fbjni.h`)
will available implicitly.

find_package(fbjni REQUIRED CONFIG)

target_link_libraries(${PACKAGE_NAME} fbjni::fbjni mylibrary)
...
## Android Build Setup (pre-4.0.0)

The Android Gradle plugin does not provide built-in support for artifacts that
include native libraries (for linking against) and header files. Because of
that, some manual additions to your build system are required. The following
is an example of what this can look like but by no means prescriptive.

In your app-specific `build.gradle`:
...
android {
  // Create new configurations that can be referred to in dependencies.
  // The Android Gradle Plugin 3.* does not allow hooking into existing
  // configurations like `implementation`.
  configurations {
    extractHeaders
    extractJNI
  }

  dependencies {
    implementation 'com.facebook.fbjni:fbjni:0.0.1'
    // If headers are required.
    extractHeaders 'com.facebook.fbjni:fbjni:0.0.1:headers'
    // If the `.so` files are required for linking.
    extractJNI 'com.facebook.fbjni:fbjni:0.0.1'
  }
}

task extractAARHeaders {
    doLast {
        configurations.extractHeaders.files.each {
            def file = it.absoluteFile
            copy {
                from zipTree(file)
                into "$buildDir/$file.name"
                include "**/*.h"
            }
        }
    }
}

task extractJNIFiles {
    doLast {
        configurations.extractJNI.files.each {
            def file = it.absoluteFile
            copy {
                from zipTree(file)
                into "$buildDir/$file.name"
                include "jni/**/*"
            }
        }
    }
}

tasks.whenTaskAdded { task ->
    if (task.name.contains('externalNativeBuild')) {
        task.dependsOn(extractAARHeaders)
        task.dependsOn(extractJNIFiles)
    }
}
...
With this setup in place, prior to any native build jobs, the header files
and JNI shared libraries will be extracted under the build directory.

Now, in your CMake setup, you can refer to the extracted paths:

```cmake
set(build_DIR ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/build)
set(PACKAGE_NAME "myapp")

file(GLOB libfbjni_link_DIRS "${build_DIR}/fbjni*.aar/jni/${ANDROID_ABI}")
file(GLOB libfbjni_include_DIRS "${build_DIR}/fbjni-*-headers.jar/")

find_library(FBJNI_LIBRARY fbjni PATHS ${libfbjni_link_DIRS}
NO_CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH)

target_include_directories(${PACKAGE_NAME} PRIVATE
  // Additional header directories here
  ${libfbjni_include_DIRS}
)
target_link_libraries(${PACKAGE_NAME} ${FBJNI_LIBRARY} mylibrary)

Title: worklets 0.12 compatibility for Expo 57
URL: https://github.com/expo/expo/issues/49225
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
# worklets 0.12 compatibility for Expo 57
...
worklets 0.12.x renamed WorkletRuntime::executeSync → runSync. But Expo SDK 57's expo-modules-core@57.0.12 WorkletsAdapter calls executeSync(...) directly, with no version guard. Expo SDK 57 officially supports only worklets 0.10.1 / reanimated 4.5.1, so your bump to worklets 0.12.1 / reanimated 4.6.0 was ahead of Expo's support and broke the adapter's compile.
...
> Why is this closed, I encountered this issue too.
> 
> Here's my patch that fixes it:
> 
> ```diff
> diff --git a/android/src/main/cpp/worklets/WorkletJSCallInvoker.cpp b/android/src/main/cpp/worklets/WorkletJSCallInvoker.cpp
> index a2d707ce76ceb35456eb075d06473ac98ad8b5eb..0a69a24b93d0d26529d331098d2d0c62696e65bb 100644
> --- a/android/src/main/cpp/worklets/WorkletJSCallInvoker.cpp
> +++ b/android/src/main/cpp/worklets/WorkletJSCallInvoker.cpp
> @@ -24,7 +24,7 @@ namespace expo {
> return;
> }
> 
> - workletRuntime->executeSync(func = std::move(func) -> jsi::Value {
> + workletRuntime->runSync(func = std::move(func) -> jsi::Value {
> func(rt);
> return jsi::Value::undefined();
> });
> diff --git a/ios/WorkletsAdapter/ExpoWorkletsBridgeProvider.mm b/ios/WorkletsAdapter/ExpoWorkletsBridgeProvider.mm
> index 126545fae12dc3af71e0ea382b976ef430e62d17..d97163a2e9a9db09f43786bc919f2fa229f21901 100644
> --- a/ios/WorkletsAdapter/ExpoWorkletsBridgeProvider.mm
> +++ b/ios/WorkletsAdapter/ExpoWorkletsBridgeProvider.mm
> @@ -233,7 +233,7 @@ - (void)executeWorkletWithRuntimeHandle:(id)runtimeHandle
> return;
> }
> 
> - workletRuntime->executeSync(worklet, arguments -> jsi::Value {
> + workletRuntime->runSync(worklet, arguments -> jsi::Value {
> return callWorklet(rt, worklet, arguments);
> });
> }
> ```

Updating to `expo@57.0.9` or later is crucial for affected apps.

We currently do not recommend it for production use until it's officially supported. If you enabled it as a workaround, update to `expo@57.0.9` or later instead.
- Increased startup time in development is resolved in `expo@57.0.17`: a Hermes V1 regression could unintentionally increase app startup time during development (expo/expo#48298). This did not affect production apps. `expo@57.0.17` updates React Native to 0.86.3, which resolves this regression.

Title: [expo-updates][Android] CMake build ignores reactNativeArchitectures and builds unused ABIs
URL: https://github.com/expo/expo/issues/49291
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
# [expo-updates][Android] CMake build ignores reactNativeArchitectures and builds unused ABIs
...
This is a source-level Android build issue in `expo-updates`; no application code is required. The current SDK 57 source and the published `expo-updates@57.0.17` tarball both reproduce the missing ABI filtering.
...
`expo-updates` should honor `reactNativeArchitectures=x86_64`, consistent with other Expo C++ modules, and configure/build CMake only for x86_64.
...
`expo-updates/android/build.gradle` declares `externalNativeBuild.cmake` but never applies `reactNativeArchitectures` as an ABI filter:

https://github.com/expo/expo/blob/sdk-57/packages/expo-updates/android/build.gradle#L89-L113

As a result, x86_64-only builds still configure/build the `expo-updates` native code for unused Android ABIs. This adds avoidable CMake/NDK work to emulator and CI builds.

Other Expo modules already handle the property. For example, `expo-modules-core`, `expo-gl`, and `expo-sqlite` define a `reactNativeArchitectures()` helper and pass it to `abiFilters`.
...
- `expo-updates@57.0.10`
- `expo-updates@57.0.11`
- `expo-updates@57.0.17` (latest at the time of filing)

A working local workaround is:

```gradle
defaultConfig {
  if (project.hasProperty("reactNativeArchitectures")) {
    ndk {
      abiFilters(*project.property("reactNativeArchitectures").split(","))
    }
  }
}
```

For consistency with other Expo modules, the upstream implementation could instead reuse their helper pattern:

```gradle
def reactNativeArchitectures() {
  def value = project.getProperties().get("reactNativeArchitectures")
  return value ? value.split(",") : ["armeabi-v7a", "x86", "x86_64", "arm64-v8a"]
}

// inside externalNativeBuild.cmake
abiFilters(*reactNativeArchitectures())
```

This is a build-performance issue rather than an APK correctness issue. Default production builds can continue building all configured ABIs; explicit single-ABI builds should not compile the others.

Title: [expo-modules-autolinking] Android `cmakeListsPath` default breaks for `isPureCxxDependency` modules
URL: https://github.com/expo/expo/issues/45057
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
`expo-modules-autolinking`'s Android resolver unconditionally sets `cmakeListsPath` to ` /build/generated/source/codegen/jni/CMakeLists.txt` — even for modules classified as `isPureCxxDependency: true`. Pure-C++ dependencies never run the codegen task that populates this directory, so the generated `Android-autolinking.cmake` emits an `add_subdirectory(...)` line pointing at a path that doesn't exist. CMake configure aborts, the Android build fails.
...
`packages/expo-modules-autolinking/src/reactNativeConfig/androidResolver.ts` lines 54-57 on `main`:

```ts
let cmakeListsPath = reactNativeConfig?.cmakeListsPath
  ? path.join(androidDir, reactNativeConfig?.cmakeListsPath)
  : path.join(androidDir, 'build/generated/source/codegen/jni/CMakeLists.txt');
```

The default is applied regardless of `isPureCxxDependency`. For pure-C++ modules, `cmakeListsPath` should be `null` (and only `cxxModuleCMakeListsPath` used).
...
Affects any library that advertises `isPureCxxDependency: true` without also providing a custom `cmakeListsPath`.

Concrete example I hit: `react-native-mmkv@^3.3.3` on Expo SDK 55 (RN 0.83.2). After `expo prebuild --platform android --clean`, `packages/mobile/android/app/build/generated/autolinking/src/main/jni/Android-autolinking.cmake` contains:

```cmake
add_subdirectory(".../mmkv/android/build/generated/source/codegen/jni/" RNMmkvSpec_autolinked_build)
add_subdirectory(".../mmkv/android/"                                    RNMmkvSpec_cxxmodule_autolinked_build)
```

The first path never exists. Build aborts in the CMake configure phase with:

```
CMake Error: add_subdirectory given source ".../mmkv/android/build/generated/source/codegen/jni/" which is not an existing directory.
```
...
For dependencies where `isPureCxxDependency` is true (detected via `cxxModuleCMakeListsModuleName/Path/HeaderName` being set and `manifest/gradle` being absent, see same file line 27-31), either:

1. Leave `cmakeListsPath` as `null` and rely on `cxxModuleCMakeListsPath` only, OR
2. Only emit the `add_subdirectory` for `cmakeListsPath` in the generated cmake when the path actually exists.
...
- expo-modules-autolinking: 55.0.12
- Expo SDK: 55
- react-native: 0.83.2
- Node: 22.14.0
- OS: Windows 11 (also affects macOS/Linux — the broken path is platform-independent)
...
The cleanest fix downstream is to not use the affected library version, or to wait for the library to upgrade away from `isPureCxxDependency: true`. In my case, upgrading `react-native-mmkv` v3 → v4 (which migrated to `react-native-nitro-modules` and no longer advertises `isPureCxxDependency`) resolved the symptom without needing any autolinker change. But that only works because mmkv had a newer version available — the underlying autolinker bug is still there for any future pure-C++ module that follows the same pattern.

How to determine which version is compatible? Open https://github.com/expo/expo/blob/sdk-54/packages/expo/bundledNativeModules.json file, jump to `sdk-XX` branch and search for `"react-native-reanimated"`.

If your project uses Expo prebuild or React Native without a framework (e.g. React Native Community CLI), you should use a version of Reanimated that is compatible with the version of React Native according to the Compatibility table.

For instance, Reanimated 4.0.x works only with React Native 0.78, 0.79, 0.80 or 0.81 and is not compatible with React Native 0.82. If you want to use Reanimated with React Native 0.82, you need to upgrade to at least 4.1.0. It is recommended to use the latest available version (in this case, 4.1.3).

CMake is a build system used to compile the C++ part of Reanimated on your machine. Make sure to use CMake `3.22.1` or newer. CMake version can be customized with `CMAKE_VERSION` environmental variable, e.g. using `set CMAKE_VERSION=3.31.1`. If not set, CMake `3.22.1` is used.

Title: [Android] ReactRootProjectPlugin drops :app:preBuild -> library preBuild dependency under --configure-on-demand, breaking codegen before CMake
URL: https://github.com/react/react-native/issues/58149
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
ReactRootProjectPlugin ... :app:preBuild -> library preBuild dependency ... --configure-on
...
`ReactRootProjectPlugin` makes `:app:preBuild` depend on every library's `preBuild` so that library codegen runs before the app's CMake configure:
...
When Gradle runs with `--configure-on-demand` (Expo CLI passes it unconditionally in `expo run:android`), a library project that has not been evaluated by the time `projectsEvaluated` fires has no `preBuild` task yet, so `findByName` returns null and the dependency is silently dropped. The app's `configureCMake ` then runs before that library's `generateCodegenArtifactsFromSchema`, and the autolinking CMake file fails with:

```
CMake Error at android/app/build/generated/autolinking/src/main/jni/Android-autolinking.cmake:19 (add_subdirectory):
  add_subdirectory given source
  ".../node_modules/react-native-sherpa-onnx/android/build/generated/source/codegen/jni/"
  which is not an existing directory.
CMake Error at .../ReactAndroid/cmake-utils/ReactNative-application.cmake:97 (target_link_libraries):
  Cannot specify link libraries for target "react_codegen_SherpaOnnxSpec"
  which is not built by this project.
```

Which libraries are affected depends on evaluation order, so it looks flaky per project. In my project `@stripe/stripe-react-native` (also a codegen TurboModule library) happened to be evaluated in time and worked, while `react-native-sherpa-onnx` was not. The same failure was reported independently against that library (XDcobra/react-native-sherpa-onnx#63) and closed as not reproducible, which fits an ordering-dependent bug.

Running the identical build without `--configure-on-demand` (`./gradlew :app:assembleDebug -PreactNativeArchitectures=arm64-v8a`) succeeds; the task log shows `:react-native-sherpa-onnx:generateCodegenArtifactsFromSchema` → `:app:preBuild` → `:app:configureCMakeDebug[arm64-v8a]`.

**Workaround** (verified): in the app's `build.gradle`, add an explicit task-path dependency, which forces on-demand configuration of that project:

```groovy

URL: https://github.com/facebookincubator/fbjni/blob/main/docs/android_setup.md
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
**These instructions require the Android Gradle Build Plugin 4.0.0 or newer
as it relies on the new prefab integration.
Check below for a pre-4.0.0 workaround.**
...
android {
  dependencies {
    implementation 'com.facebook.fbjni:fbjni:0.2.2'
  }
}
...
Now, in your CMake setup, you can refer to the `fbjni` package. The header files (e.g. `fbjni.h`)
will available implicitly.
...
find_package(fbjni REQUIRED CONFIG)

target_link_libraries(${PACKAGE_NAME} fbjni::fbjni mylibrary)
...
## Android Build Setup (pre-4.0.0)

The Android Gradle plugin does not provide built-in support for artifacts that
include native libraries (for linking against) and header files. Because of
that, some manual additions to your build system are required. The following
is an example of what this can look like but by no means prescriptive.

In your app-specific `build.gradle`:
...
android {
  // Create new configurations that can be referred to in dependencies.
  // The Android Gradle Plugin 3.* does not allow hooking into existing
  // configurations like `implementation`.
  configurations {
    extractHeaders
    extractJNI
  }

  dependencies {
    implementation 'com.facebook.fbjni:fbjni:0.0.1'
    // If headers are required.
    extractHeaders 'com.facebook.fbjni:fbjni:0.0.1:headers'
    // If the `.so` files are required for linking.
    extractJNI 'com.facebook.fbjni:fbjni:0.0.1'
  }
}

task extractAARHeaders {
    doLast {
        configurations.extractHeaders.files.each {
            def file = it.absoluteFile
            copy {
                from zipTree(file)
                into "$buildDir/$file.name"
                include "**/*.h"
            }
        }
    }
}

task extractJNIFiles {
    doLast {
        configurations.extractJNI.files.each {
            def file = it.absoluteFile
            copy {
                from zipTree(file)
                into "$buildDir/$file.name"
                include "jni/**/*"
            }
        }
    }
}

tasks.whenTaskAdded { task ->
    if (task.name.contains('externalNativeBuild')) {
        task.dependsOn(extractAARHeaders)
        task.dependsOn(extractJNIFiles)
    }
}
...
With this setup in place, prior to any native build jobs, the header files
and JNI shared libraries will be extracted under the build directory.

Now, in your CMake setup, you can refer to the extracted paths:

```cmake
set(build_DIR ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/build)
set(PACKAGE_NAME "myapp")

file(GLOB libfbjni_link_DIRS "${build_DIR}/fbjni*.aar/jni/${ANDROID_ABI}")
file(GLOB libfbjni_include_DIRS "${build_DIR}/fbjni-*-headers.jar/")

find_library(FBJNI_LIBRARY fbjni PATHS ${libfbjni_link_DIRS}
NO_CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH)

target_include_directories(${PACKAGE_NAME} PRIVATE
  // Additional header directories here
  ${libfbjni_include_DIRS}
)
target_link_libraries(${PACKAGE_NAME} ${FBJNI_LIBRARY} mylibrary)

...
The `buildscripts` directory now contains the CMake package definitions:
...
If you have multiple Prefab packages, pass each package directory to the same `prefab` command and it will generate CMake packages for each.

To expose these packages to CMake, use `CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH`. For example:

```
$ cmake \
    -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=$NDK/build/cmake/android.toolchain.cmake \
    -DCMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH=buildscripts \
    -DANDROID_ABI=arm64-v8a \
    -DANDROID_PLATFORM=android-21 \
    -DANDROID_STL=c++_shared \
    $PATH_TO_CMAKE_PROJECT_SRC

```

CMake will search the `buildscripts` directory for packages when using `find_package`.

```
find_package(googletest REQUIRED CONFIG)

add_library(app_test SHARED app_test.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app_test googletest::googletest)

Android, iOS, tvOS

`expo-build-properties` is a [config plugin](https://docs.expo.dev/config-plugins/introduction.md) configuring the native build properties of your **android/gradle.properties** and **ios/Podfile.properties.json** directories during [Prebuild](https://docs.expo.dev/workflow/continuous-native-generation.md).

> This config plugin configures how [Prebuild command](https://docs.expo.dev/workflow/continuous-native-generation.md#usage) generates the native **android** and **ios** directories and therefore cannot be used with projects that don't run `npx expo prebuild` (bare projects).

## Installation

```sh
# npm
npx expo install expo-build-properties

# yarn
yarn expo install expo-build-properties

# pnpm
pnpm expo install expo-build-properties

# bun
bun expo install expo-build-properties
```

If you are installing this in an [existing React Native app](https://docs.expo.dev/bare/overview.md), make sure to [install `expo`](https://docs.expo.dev/bare/installing-expo-modules.md) in your project.

## Usage

### Example app.json with config plugin

#### app.json

```json app.json
{
  "expo": {
    "plugins": [
      [
        "expo-build-properties",
        {
          "android": {
            "compileSdkVersion": 36,
            "targetSdkVersion": 36,
            "buildToolsVersion": "36.0.0"
          },
          "ios": {
            "deploymentTarget": "16.4"
          }
        }
      ]
    ]
  }
}
```

#### app.config.js

```js app.config.js
export default {
  expo: {
    plugins: [
      [
        'expo-build-properties',
        {
          android: {
            compileSdkVersion: 36,
            targetSdkVersion: 36,
            buildToolsVersion: '36.0.0',
          },
          ios: {
            deploymentTarget: '16.4',
          },
        },
      ],
    ],
  },
};
```

### All configurable properties

[`PluginConfigType`](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v57.0.0/sdk/build-properties.md#pluginconfigtype) interface represents currently available configuration properties.

Ejecuté la regeneración y las compilaciones. **La app todavía no compila**:

- `expo prebuild --platform android --clean` terminó correctamente.
- `expo run:android` volvió a fallar al configurar CMake, al no encontrar `fbjniConfig.cmake` ni `ReactAndroidConfig.cmake`.
- También probé Gradle directamente, sin caché y sin configuración bajo demanda. Falló igual; no parece ser un problema de `.cxx` antiguo ni de esas opciones de Expo.
- Verifiqué que Gradle sí resuelve `fbjni 0.7.0` y `react-android 0.86.3`, y que los AAR contienen Prefab. El fallo está en que CMake no encuentra esos paquetes en su ruta de búsqueda.

El indicio más claro del entorno es la advertencia **CXX5304**: CMake 3.22.1 encuentra archivos del SDK en formato XML v4, que no reconoce. Además, no encontré `sdkmanager.bat` en el SDK para actualizar las herramientas desde la terminal. La regeneración también pasó del NDK 26.1 al 27.1.12297006; el error persistió con ambos, así que el NDK no parece ser la causa directa.

**Siguiente paso:** en Android Studio abre **Tools → SDK Manager → SDK Tools** e instala **Android SDK Command-line Tools (latest)** y **CMake 3.30.5**; verifica que siga instalado el NDK **27.1.12297006**. Después, el plugin de `expo-build-properties` permite configurar `"cmakeVersion": "3.30.5"` para el proyecto Android; su opción `ndkVersion` actual no aparece entre las admitidas por la documentación de SDK 57, por eso `prebuild --clean` regeneró con el NDK predeterminado de React Native.

`expo-doctor` pasó 19 de 21 comprobaciones; las dos incidencias fueron la conexión a Expo y una configuración de Metro, no estos errores nativos. No quedaron cambios en archivos versionados.

content.text:
No; Android permite instalar varias versiones de CMake en paralelo. En Android Studio, ve a **Tools → SDK Manager → SDK Tools**, activa **Show Package Details** y revisa las versiones disponibles bajo **CMake**. Puedes instalar una anterior sin quitar la 4.1.2.

**No necesitas bajar de versión todavía:** primero probaría la 4.1.2 que ya instalaste. Tenerla instalada no significa que Gradle la use automáticamente; el proyecto debe seleccionarla. En `apps/mobile/app.json`, cambia la opción `ndkVersion` del plugin por `cmakeVersion`:

```json
[
  "expo-build-properties",
  {
    "android": {
      "cmakeVersion": "4.1.2"
    }
  }
]
```

Luego regenera y compila:

```powershell
npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo prebuild --platform android --clean
npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo run:android
```

Si aparece un error nuevo de compatibilidad con CMake 4.1.2, prueba una versión 3.x que aparezca en **Show Package Details** y configura ese número en `cmakeVersion`. La compilación anterior seguía invocando CMake 3.22.1; instalar otra versión por sí solo no la selecciona.
Voy a ejecutar la regeneración limpia y después la compilación. Revisaré en la salida qué versiones de CMake y NDK termina usando Gradle.

# Project-wide Gradle settings.

# IDE (e.g. Android Studio) users:
# Gradle settings configured through the IDE *will override*
# any settings specified in this file.

# For more details on how to configure your build environment visit
# http://www.gradle.org/docs/current/userguide/build_environment.html

# Specifies the JVM arguments used for the daemon process.
# The setting is particularly useful for tweaking memory settings.
# Default value: -Xmx512m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m
org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx2048m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m

# When configured, Gradle will run in incubating parallel mode.
# This option should only be used with decoupled projects. More details, visit
# http://www.gradle.org/docs/current/userguide/multi_project_builds.html#sec:decoupled_projects
org.gradle.parallel=true

# AndroidX package structure to make it clearer which packages are bundled with the
# Android operating system, and which are packaged with your app's APK
# https://developer.android.com/topic/libraries/support-library/androidx-rn
android.useAndroidX=true

# Enable AAPT2 PNG crunching
android.enablePngCrunchInReleaseBuilds=true

# Use this property to specify which architecture you want to build.
# You can also override it from the CLI using
# ./gradlew <task> -PreactNativeArchitectures=x86_64
reactNativeArchitectures=armeabi-v7a,arm64-v8a,x86,x86_64

# Use this property to enable support to the new architecture.
# This will allow you to use TurboModules and the Fabric render in
# your application. You should enable this flag either if you want
# to write custom TurboModules/Fabric components OR use libraries that
# are providing them.
newArchEnabled=true

# Use this property to enable or disable the Hermes JS engine.
# If set to false, you will be using JSC instead.
hermesEnabled=true

# Use this property to enable edge-to-edge display support.
# This allows your app to draw behind system bars for an immersive UI.
# Note: Only works with ReactActivity and should not be used with custom Activity.
edgeToEdgeEnabled=true

# Enable GIF support in React Native images (~200 B increase)
expo.gif.enabled=true
# Enable webp support in React Native images (~85 KB increase)
expo.webp.enabled=true
# Enable animated webp support (~3.4 MB increase)
# Disabled by default because iOS doesn't support animated webp
expo.webp.animated=false

# Enable network inspector
EX_DEV_CLIENT_NETWORK_INSPECTOR=true

# Use legacy packaging to compress native libraries in the resulting APK.
expo.useLegacyPackaging=false

expo.inlineModules.watchedDirectories=[]
android.cmakeVersion=4.1.2

content.text:
Retomé la compilación. **La regeneración funcionó, pero el ensamblado aún falla**:

- `expo run:android` no llegó a Gradle porque el emulador `Pixel_4` rechazó la conexión al puerto 5554.
- Para probar la compilación sin depender del emulador, ejecuté `app:assembleDebug` directamente. Falló en los mismos `find_package` de `ReactAndroid` y `fbjni`.
- Confirmé que ahora sí se está usando **CMake 4.1.2**. También vi que Gradle ejecuta Prefab con los paquetes `react-android 0.86.3` y `fbjni 0.7.0` y devuelve código 0; después, CMake no encuentra sus archivos de configuración. Así que instalar o seleccionar otra versión de CMake no ha corregido el problema.
- El NDK utilizado fue **27.1.12297006**, no el 26.1 de `app.json`: esa opción no se está aplicando en esta regeneración.
- Sigue apareciendo la advertencia `CXX5304` sobre SDK XML v4.

El punto pendiente está entre la salida de Prefab que prepara Gradle y la ruta donde CMake intenta buscarla. No es que falten las dependencias en Gradle, y **la compilación todavía no está lista**. Para volver a probar `expo run:android`, primero habrá que iniciar `Pixel_4` desde Device Manager; eso resolverá el bloqueo del emulador, pero no el error de Prefab.

content.text:
El siguiente paso es probar **CMake 3.30.5**, que ya está instalado y aparece en el registro de Gradle. La 4.1.2 se seleccionó correctamente, pero el fallo de Prefab continuó.

En `app.json`, deja el plugin así; quita `ndkVersion` porque el prebuild no lo está aplicando y React Native está usando su NDK predeterminado, **27.1.12297006**:

```json
[
  "expo-build-properties",
  {
    "android": {
      "cmakeVersion": "3.30.5"
    }
  }
]
```

Después, primero regenera y compila directamente con Gradle —esto evita que el emulador interfiera con la prueba—:

```powershell
npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo prebuild --platform android --clean
.\apps\mobile\android\gradlew.bat app:assembleDebug -x lint -x test --no-configure-on-demand -PreactNativeArchitectures=x86_64
```

Si Gradle termina bien, inicia `Pixel_4` desde **Android Studio → Device Manager** y ejecuta `npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo run:android`. La última vez Expo se detuvo antes de compilar porque el emulador no respondía en el puerto 5554; el ensamblado directo permite comprobar CMake primero.

Ese error es solo porque ejecutaste Gradle desde la raíz del repositorio, donde no hay un `settings.gradle`. **La compilación ni siquiera llegó a CMake.**

Desde la raíz, ejecuta el mismo comando indicando el directorio Android con `-p`:

```

Así Gradle buscará la configuración en `apps\mobile\android`. Después comparte el primer error que aparezca, si falla.

content.text:
Gracias. **Esta prueba confirma que CMake 3.30.5 sí se está usando, pero cambiar la versión no resolvió el fallo.** El ABI ahora también es correcto (`x86_64`). No hace falta seguir alternando versiones de CMake ni iniciar el emulador para diagnosticarlo.

El error continúa en la preparación de **Prefab**: CMake busca `ReactAndroidConfig.cmake` y `fbjniConfig.cmake` en las carpetas `.cxx` de `react-native-screens` y `react-native-worklets`, pero no los encuentra. En una ejecución anterior, Gradle sí resolvió los AAR de React Native y fbjni, así que la investigación debe enfocarse en cómo Gradle prepara y entrega esos archivos a CMake.

El siguiente paso es inspeccionar la salida temporal de Prefab y compararla con la ruta `CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH` que aparece en el error. Con eso se puede determinar si Gradle no está generando los archivos esperados o si los genera en otra ruta, antes de decidir qué configuración corregir.

¡Bien! La prueba de `react-native-screens` **terminó con `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`** y encontró `ReactAndroidConfig.cmake` en la ruta Prefab esperada. Es una buena señal: esas dos líneas finales del script no imprimieron nada porque solo muestran mensajes cuando no se encuentra la configuración; al encontrarla, es normal que queden silenciosas.

Ahora prueba el ensamblado completo, que también permitirá confirmar si `react-native-worklets` encuentra `fbjni`:

```powershell
.\apps\mobile\android\gradlew.bat -p .\apps\mobile\android app:assembleDebug -x lint -x test --no-configure-on-demand -PreactNativeArchitectures=x86_64
```

No necesita un emulador para compilar. Si termina en `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, inicia `Pixel_4` desde Device Manager y luego ejecuta `npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo run:android`. Si falla, compárteme el primer bloque `Task failed`, especialmente si menciona `react-native-worklets` o `fbjni`.

¡La compilación ya pasó! El problema actual es distinto: **ADB ve el emulador como `offline`**, así que Expo no puede consultar sus propiedades ni instalar la app. Que Pixel 4 aparezca encendido no garantiza que ADB ya esté listo.

En PowerShell, desde cualquier carpeta, revisa su estado:

```powershell
$adb = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\platform-tools\adb.exe"
& $adb devices -l
```

Si aparece `emulator-5554 offline`, reinicia ADB:

```powershell
& $adb kill-server
& $adb start-server
& $adb devices -l
```

Si aún figura `offline`, en Android Studio abre **Device Manager → Pixel 4 → ⋮ → Cold Boot Now** y vuelve a revisar `adb devices -l`. Debe aparecer como `device`. Entonces ejecuta de nuevo:

```powershell
npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo run:android
```

No hace falta repetir `prebuild` ni la compilación de CMake; ese paso ya terminó correctamente.

## Expo has changed — do not trust your training data

Expo ships breaking changes every SDK release. APIs you remember are likely renamed, moved, or removed. Before writing any code that touches an Expo, EAS, or React Native API:

1. Read the major version of the `expo` package in `package.json`.
2. Fetch the matching versioned docs: `https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v<major>.0.0/`
3. For anything else, fetch https://docs.expo.dev/llms.txt — an index of all Expo docs with corrections to common LLM misconceptions. Follow its links to the specific page you need; never answer from memory.

## Commands

Use `bunx` instead of `npx` if the project uses bun (`bun.lock` present).

```bash
npx expo install <package>  # ALWAYS use instead of npm/yarn/pnpm/bun add — resolves SDK-compatible versions
npx expo start              # start the dev server
npx expo lint               # lint
npx tsc --noEmit            # typecheck
npx expo-doctor             # diagnose dependency and config issues
npx expo install --fix      # fix incompatible package versions
```

Run lint and typecheck before declaring any task done.

## Navigation & Routing

- Use **Expo Router** for all navigation. Routes live in `src/app/` — every file there is a screen, `_layout.tsx` files define navigators. Keep non-route code (components, hooks, utils) outside `src/app/`.
- Import `Link`, `router`, and `useLocalSearchParams` from `expo-router`.
- Docs: https://docs.expo.dev/router/introduction.md

## Building with EAS

Use EAS to build, sign, and submit the app in the cloud (`eas build`, `eas submit`) and to ship over-the-air updates (`eas update`) — no local Xcode or Android Studio required. Run EAS CLI as `bunx eas-cli <command>` in Bun projects, or `npx eas-cli@latest <command>` otherwise; substitute that for bare `eas` in docs examples.
Docs: https://docs.expo.dev/eas/index.md

## Rules

- If `ios/` and `android/` directories do not exist, they are generated (Continuous Native Generation). Never create or edit them by hand — configure native behavior in `app.json` and config plugins.
- Expo Go only includes its bundled native modules. After adding a library with native code, the app needs a development build: `npx expo run:ios|android` locally, or `eas build --profile development`.

*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: apps/mobile/ANDROID_BUILD.md
+# Compilar Android en Windows
+
+Guía para instalar y ejecutar la app móvil desde este monorepo en una PC Windows. Los comandos se ejecutan desde la **raíz del repositorio** (`al-toque-delivery`), salvo que se indique otra cosa.
+
+## Versiones usadas por este proyecto
+
+El proyecto utiliza Expo SDK 57 y React Native 0.86.3. La configuración Android comprobada es:
+
+| Componente | Versión |
+| --- | --- |
+| Node.js | 22.13 o posterior |
+| Java para Gradle | JDK compatible con Gradle 9.3.1; se recomienda el JDK de Android Studio |
+| Android SDK Platform | 36 |
+| Android SDK Build-Tools | 36.0.0 |
+| Android NDK | 27.1.12297006, seleccionado por Expo/React Native |
+| CMake | 3.30.5, fijado en `app.json` con `expo-build-properties` |
+| Arquitectura del emulador | `x86_64` |
+
+No hace falta agregar `ndkVersion` a `expo-build-properties` para esta configuración. Después de `prebuild`, Gradle informa el NDK seleccionado; en esta app es `27.1.12297006`.
+
+## Preparación de una PC nueva
+
+1. Instala Node.js 22.13 o posterior y Android Studio.
+2. En Android Studio abre **Tools → SDK Manager → SDK Platforms** e instala Android SDK Platform 36.
+3. En **SDK Tools**, instala o verifica:
+   - Android SDK Build-Tools 36.0.0
+   - Android SDK Command-line Tools (latest)
+   - Android Emulator y Android SDK Platform-Tools
+   - CMake 3.30.5
+   - NDK (Side by side) 27.1.12297006
+4. En **Tools → Device Manager**, crea o inicia un emulador Android x86_64.
+5. Desde la raíz del repositorio instala las dependencias:
+
+   ```powershell
+   npm ci
+   ```
+
+6. Configura los archivos locales que necesita el proyecto antes de compilar:
+   - `.env` en la raíz del monorepo, con las variables requeridas por la app.
+   - `apps/mobile/google-services.json`, para Firebase en Android.
+
+   No copies valores secretos a este documento ni los subas al repositorio.
+
+## Compilar e instalar en el emulador
+
+Inicia el emulador en Device Manager y comprueba que ADB lo vea como `device`:
+
+```powershell
+$adb = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\platform-tools\adb.exe"
+& $adb devices -l
+```
+
+La fila del emulador debe terminar en `device`, por ejemplo:
+
+```text
+emulator-5554    device
+```
+
+En una instalación inicial, o después de cambiar la configuración nativa en `app.json`, regenera Android:
+
+```powershell
+npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo prebuild --platform android --clean
+```
+
+`--clean` elimina y vuelve a generar `apps/mobile/android`. No lo ejecutes si conservas cambios manuales dentro de esa carpeta que no estén definidos mediante `app.json` o plugins.
+
+Después compila, instala y abre la app:
+
+```powershell
+npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo run:android
+```
+
+En el primer build Gradle puede tardar varios minutos. El resultado esperado incluye `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, la instalación de `app-debug.apk` y el inicio de Metro.
+
+## Compilar sin iniciar un emulador
+
+Para comprobar el ensamblado Android sin instalar ni abrir la app, usa Gradle desde la raíz con `-p` apuntando al proyecto nativo:
+
+```powershell
+.\apps\mobile\android\gradlew.bat -p .\apps\mobile\android app:assembleDebug -x lint -x test --no-configure-on-demand -PreactNativeArchitectures=x86_64
+```
+
+El APK debug se genera en:
+
+```text
+apps/mobile/android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
+```
+
+`x86_64` debe escribirse completo. `x86_6` no es un ABI válido.
+
+## Si ADB muestra el emulador como `offline`
+
+Que la ventana del emulador esté abierta no garantiza que ADB esté conectado. Reinicia ADB:
+
+```powershell
+$adb = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\platform-tools\adb.exe"
+& $adb kill-server
+& $adb start-server
+& $adb devices -l
+```
+
+Si sigue como `offline`, abre **Android Studio → Device Manager**, selecciona el emulador y usa **Cold Boot Now**. Confirma que después aparezca como `device` y vuelve a ejecutar `expo run:android`.
+
+## Si vuelve el error de CMake/Prefab
+
+Los errores de `fbjniConfig.cmake` o `ReactAndroidConfig.cmake` ocurren durante la configuración C++ de `react-native-worklets` o `react-native-screens`. Para esta app:
+
+1. Comprueba que `apps/mobile/app.json` conserve `cmakeVersion: "3.30.5"` dentro del plugin `expo-build-properties`.
+2. Verifica en Android Studio SDK Manager que CMake 3.30.5 y NDK 27.1.12297006 estén instalados.
+3. Regenera el proyecto nativo y prueba primero el ensamblado sin emulador:
+
+   ```powershell
+   npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo prebuild --platform android --clean
+   .\apps\mobile\android\gradlew.bat -p .\apps\mobile\android app:assembleDebug -x lint -x test --no-configure-on-demand -PreactNativeArchitectures=x86_64
+   ```
+
+4. Si falla, conserva el **primer** error `CMake Error` y la línea `CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH`; las advertencias de Kotlin, la advertencia Gradle sobre futuras versiones y los mensajes de DevTools no sustituyen ese error principal.
+
+## Avisos que no necesariamente indican un fallo
+
+- `Waiting for a DevTools connection` o `No compatible apps connected` se refieren al depurador JavaScript. Si la app se abrió y funciona, no impiden la compilación.
+- `expo run:android` necesita que ADB detecte el emulador para instalar y abrir la app. `gradlew app:assembleDebug` permite compilar sin emulador.

display.text:
# Compilar Android en Windows

Guía para instalar y ejecutar la app móvil desde este monorepo en una PC Windows. Los comandos se ejecutan desde la **raíz del repositorio** (`al-toque-delivery`), salvo que se indique otra cosa.

## Versiones usadas por este proyecto

El proyecto utiliza Expo SDK 57 y React Native 0.86.3. La configuración Android comprobada es:

| Componente | Versión |
| --- | --- |
| Node.js | 22.13 o posterior |
| Java para Gradle | JDK compatible con Gradle 9.3.1; se recomienda el JDK de Android Studio |
| Android SDK Platform | 36 |
| Android SDK Build-Tools | 36.0.0 |
| Android NDK | 27.1.12297006, seleccionado por Expo/React Native |
| CMake | 3.30.5, fijado en `app.json` con `expo-build-properties` |
| Arquitectura del emulador | `x86_64` |

No hace falta agregar `ndkVersion` a `expo-build-properties` para esta configuración. Después de `prebuild`, Gradle informa el NDK seleccionado; en esta app es `27.1.12297006`.

## Preparación de una PC nueva

1. Instala Node.js 22.13 o posterior y Android Studio.
2. En Android Studio abre **Tools → SDK Manager → SDK Platforms** e instala Android SDK Platform 36.
3. En **SDK Tools**, instala o verifica:
   - Android SDK Build-Tools 36.0.0
   - Android SDK Command-line Tools (latest)
   - Android Emulator y Android SDK Platform-Tools
   - CMake 3.30.5
   - NDK (Side by side) 27.1.12297006
4. En **Tools → Device Manager**, crea o inicia un emulador Android x86_64.
5. Desde la raíz del repositorio instala las dependencias:

   ```powershell
   npm ci
   ```

6. Configura los archivos locales que necesita el proyecto antes de compilar:
   - `.env` en la raíz del monorepo, con las variables requeridas por la app.
   - `apps/mobile/google-services.json`, para Firebase en Android.

   No copies valores secretos a este documento ni los subas al repositorio.

## Compilar e instalar en el emulador

Inicia el emulador en Device Manager y comprueba que ADB lo vea como `device`:

```powershell
$adb = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\platform-tools\adb.exe"
& $adb devices -l
```

La fila del emulador debe terminar en `device`, por ejemplo:

```text
emulator-5554    device
```

En una instalación inicial, o después de cambiar la configuración nativa en `app.json`, regenera Android:

```powershell
npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo prebuild --platform android --clean
```

`--clean` elimina y vuelve a generar `apps/mobile/android`. No lo ejecutes si conservas cambios manuales dentro de esa carpeta que no estén definidos mediante `app.json` o plugins.

Después compila, instala y abre la app:

```powershell
npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo run:android
```

En el primer build Gradle puede tardar varios minutos. El resultado esperado incluye `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, la instalación de `app-debug.apk` y el inicio de Metro.

## Compilar sin iniciar un emulador

Para comprobar el ensamblado Android sin instalar ni abrir la app, usa Gradle desde la raíz con `-p` apuntando al proyecto nativo:

```powershell
.\apps\mobile\android\gradlew.bat -p .\apps\mobile\android app:assembleDebug -x lint -x test --no-configure-on-demand -PreactNativeArchitectures=x86_64
```

El APK debug se genera en:

```text
apps/mobile/android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
```

`x86_64` debe escribirse completo. `x86_6` no es un ABI válido.

## Si ADB muestra el emulador como `offline`

Que la ventana del emulador esté abierta no garantiza que ADB esté conectado. Reinicia ADB:

```powershell
$adb = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\platform-tools\adb.exe"
& $adb kill-server
& $adb start-server
& $adb devices -l
```

Si sigue como `offline`, abre **Android Studio → Device Manager**, selecciona el emulador y usa **Cold Boot Now**. Confirma que después aparezca como `device` y vuelve a ejecutar `expo run:android`.

## Si vuelve el error de CMake/Prefab

Los errores de `fbjniConfig.cmake` o `ReactAndroidConfig.cmake` ocurren durante la configuración C++ de `react-native-worklets` o `react-native-screens`. Para esta app:

1. Comprueba que `apps/mobile/app.json` conserve `cmakeVersion: "3.30.5"` dentro del plugin `expo-build-properties`.
2. Verifica en Android Studio SDK Manager que CMake 3.30.5 y NDK 27.1.12297006 estén instalados.
3. Regenera el proyecto nativo y prueba primero el ensamblado sin emulador:

   ```powershell
   npm exec --workspace=apps/mobile -- expo prebuild --platform android --clean
   .\apps\mobile\android\gradlew.bat -p .\apps\mobile\android app:assembleDebug -x lint -x test --no-configure-on-demand -PreactNativeArchitectures=x86_64
   ```

4. Si falla, conserva el **primer** error `CMake Error` y la línea `CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH`; las advertencias de Kotlin, la advertencia Gradle sobre futuras versiones y los mensajes de DevTools no sustituyen ese error principal.

## Avisos que no necesariamente indican un fallo

- `Waiting for a DevTools connection` o `No compatible apps connected` se refieren al depurador JavaScript. Si la app se abrió y funciona, no impiden la compilación.
- `expo run:android` necesita que ADB detecte el emulador para instalar y abrir la app. `gradlew app:assembleDebug` permite compilar sin emulador.

URL: https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/issues/7317
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
When running ./gradlew clean build without --refresh-dependencies, the build fails on the second attempt with the error:

> Error: invalid value for <package_path>: directory ".../node_modules/react-native-reanimated/android/build/intermediates/prefab_package/debug/prefab" is not readable

The error occurs because the prefab directory becomes corrupted or inaccessible between builds. Manually deleting directories or using --refresh-dependencies temporarily fixes the issue, but this is not sustainable for CI/CD pipelines.

Published: N/A

Highlights:
This PR adds precompiled ... (PCH) ... the Android CMake builds for
`libre ... .so` and `libworklets.so ... clang parse the
...
stable-third ... party headers (`folly/dynamic.h ... `jsi/js ... .h`, `fbjni.h
...
RN renderer headers, C++ standard library) ... per build instead
...
`target_precompile_headers` causes CMake to generate `cmake_pch.hxx` (a
wrapper that `#include`s every header listed in `*PCH.h`), build it once
into a `cmake_pch.hxx.pch` binary, and force-include the wrapper via
`-Xclang -include -Xclang …cmake_pch.hxx` in every TU compile command
(clang transparently loads the paired `.pch`). clang emits `.d`
dependency files for both the PCH compile and each TU; ninja stores
these and stats every recorded path on each build. If anything
transitively pulled in by the PCH changed mtime, the `.pch` is rebuilt —
and because every TU depends on the `.pch`, they all rebuild too.

| Scenario | What rebuilds | Cost vs no-PCH |
|---|---|---|
| Edit a Reanimated/Worklets `.cpp` | Just that TU | Same |
| Edit a Reanimated/Worklets `.h` not in PCH | Every TU that includes it
| Same |
| Edit `*PCH.h` itself | PCH binary + every TU in that lib | Same as a
clean lib build |
| RN patch bump (same prefab transform hash) | Usually nothing | Same |
| RN minor bump | PCH binary + every TU | Same as today (RN bumps
already invalidate every TU because prefab include paths are part of
compile commands) |
| NDK / libc++ update | PCH binary + every TU | Same as today |
| Compile-flag change (feature flag macro, build type) | PCH binary +
every TU | Same as today |

PCH never adds invalidation — it only adds an extra build artifact that
recompiles in lock-step with the things that already trigger a full
rebuild. The invariant is: any change that previously forced a clean lib
rebuild still does, plus a ~1–2 s PCH compile, then every TU is faster.

clang refuses to load a PCH built with mismatched flags (different
language standard, target, defines, etc.) — it errors `module file built
with different flags` rather than silently producing wrong code. So a
stale `.pch` is a build failure, not a runtime bug.

The PCH binary lives inside
`.cxx/ / / /CMakeFiles/.dir/` and is wiped by
`gradlew clean` and the existing `cleanCMakeCache` task — no new
maintenance.
...
Enabling PCH causes Android Studio's Gradle Sync to surface a C++
indexer error on a clean checkout — the IDE can't index sources without
the precompiled header binary (`cmake_pch.hxx.pch`), which doesn't exist
until the first build. The project compiles fine; the failure is
sync-only.

 

To unblock sync **without making sync slower**, both packages apply
`generate-stub-pch.gradle.kts`. After `configureCMakeDebug`, it walks
`compile_commands.json` and compiles a **stub `.pch` from an empty
header** for every ABI. Generating the real PCH here would defeat the
purpose — it'd push several seconds of full PCH compile into every sync.
The stub satisfies the indexer, and its mtime is backdated below
`cmake_pch.hxx.cxx` so the next real build invokes ninja to regenerate
the proper PCH binary in the normal build pipeline.

Title: 0fd3b10 Workaround AGP/prefab issue on native dependency resolution. (Claude)
URL: https://github.com/atsushieno/aap-core/commit/0fd3b1064a313a23895303e43244a82f0773a59f
Published: 2026-05-12T12:00:32.000Z
Author: atsushieno
Highlights:
Root cause (AGP/prefab bug):

When configureCMakeDebug runs for androidaudioplugin-midi-device-service or
androidaudioplugin-manager, AGP only declares a dependency on
prefabDebugConfigurePackage (which writes a JSON metadata file), not on
prefabDebugPackage (which actually creates the prefab package including
the .so).
If configureCMakeDebug runs before the .so is in the prefab package, the
prefab CLI generates an INTERFACE IMPORTED cmake target (header-only)
instead of SHARED IMPORTED — and AGP doesn't detect this is stale because
it tracks the JSON metadata, not the .so content.
...
```diff
@@ -72,6 +72,23 @@ dependencies {
     androidTestImplementation (libs.test.espresso.core)
 }
 
+// Workaround for AGP/prefab issue: cmake for consuming modules may generate INTERFACE IMPORTED
+// targets when the producing module's .so hasn't been built yet at configure time.
+// AGP only tracks prefab_publication.json (not .so content) for cmake cache invalidation,
+// so we explicitly order configure after the prefab package task (which contains the .so).
+// See also: https://issuetracker.google.com/issues/385751152
+gradle.projectsEvaluated {
+    val aapProject = rootProject.project("androidaudioplugin")
+    tasks.matching { it.name.startsWith("configureCMakeDebug") }.configureEach {
+        dependsOn(aapProject.tasks["prefabDebugPackage"])
+    }
+    tasks.matching { it.name.startsWith("configureCMakeRelWithDebInfo") }.configureEach {
+        dependsOn(aapProject.tasks["prefabReleasePackage"])
+    }
+    tasks["buildCMakeDebug"].dependsOn(aapProject.tasks["mergeDebugNativeLibs"])
+    tasks["buildCMakeRelWithDebInfo"].dependsOn(aapProject.tasks["mergeReleaseNativeLibs"])
+}
+
 
 val gitProjectName = "aap-core"
 val packageName = project.name

AAR libraries can contain native dependencies that the Android Gradle Plugin can consume. AGP is also capable of producing AARs that expose native libraries to their consumers.
...
Starting with Android Gradle plugin 4.0, C/C++ dependencies can be imported from AARs linked in your `build.gradle` file. Gradle will automatically make these available to the native build system, but your build system must be configured to make use of the imported libraries and headers. Since C/C++ dependencies are distributed as AARs, the following links about generic AARs may be helpful:
...
AAR dependencies of your Gradle modules can expose native libraries for use by your application. Inside the AAR, the `prefab` directory contains a Prefab package, which includes the headers and libraries of the native dependency.
...
The `prefab` feature must be enabled for your Android Gradle module.
...
Dependencies imported from an AAR are exposed to CMake via CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH. This value will be set automatically by Gradle when CMake is invoked, so if your build modifies this variable be sure to append rather than assign to it.

Each dependency exposes a config-file package to your build. These are imported with the find_package command. This command searches for config-file packages matching the given package name and version and exposes the targets it defines to be used in your build. For example, if your application defines `lib ... .so` and it uses cURL, your `CMakeLists.txt` should include the following:
...
The ability to create native AARs was first added in AGP 4.1.

To export your native libraries, add the following to the `android` block of your library project's `build.gradle.kts` file:

### Kotlin

buildFeatures { prefabPublishing = true} prefab { create(

mylibrary

) { headers = 

"src/main/cpp/

mylibrary

 } create(

myotherlibrary

) { headers = 

"src/main/cpp/

myotherlibrary

mylibrary

"src/main/cpp/

mylibrary

myotherlibrary

"src/main/cpp/

myotherlibrary

 }}

In this example, the `mylibrary` and `myotherlibrary` libraries from either your ndk-build or CMake external native build will be packaged in the AAR produced by your build, and each will export the headers from the specified directory to their dependents.

33:       // function to check if property is set.

### 如何设置或找到 HDF5 的 INCLUDE_DIRS 路径 在 CMake 中，find_package(HDF5 REQUIRED) 是用于定位 HDF5 库及其头文件的关键命令。一旦成功调用了 find_package 命令并找到了 HDF5，CMake 将会定义一些变量来存储库路径和头文件路径的信息。 #### 使用 CMake 查找 HDF5 头文件路径 可以通过以下方式获取 HDF5 的头文件路径： 1. **通过 CMake 缓存查看** 如果已经运行过 cmake 并且成功配置了项目，则可以检查生成的缓存文件中的变量 ${HDF5_INCLUDE_DIRS} 或者类似的变量名（具体取决于版本）。这些变量通常会被打印出来或者记录在日志中。 2. **手动查询变量** 可以在项目的根目录下创建一个简单的脚本文件（例如 FindHDF5Path.cmake），内容如下： cmake cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.0) project(FindHDF5) find_package(HDF5 REQUIRED COMPONENTS CXX) if (HDF5_FOUND) message(STATUS "HDF5 Include Directories: ${HDF5_INCLUDE_DIRS}") message(STATUS "HDF5 Libraries: ${HDF5_LIBRARIES}") endif() 运行此脚本时，执行以下命令即可显示 HDF5 的头文件路径： bash mkdir build && cd build cmake .. 输出将会类似于下面的内容： -- HDF5 Include Directories: /usr/local/include/hdf5/serial/ -- HDF5 Libraries: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libhdf5.so;/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libhdf5_cpp.so 3. **直接使用 locate 工具** 如果系统上安装了 mlocate 工具，可以直接通过 locate hdf5.h 来快速查找该文件的位置。例如，在某些 Linux 发行版中，可能返回的结果为 /usr/include/hdf5/serial/hdf5.h[^3]。 4. **环境变量辅助** 在某些情况下，如果系统的默认路径未能被自动检测到，可以尝试设置环境变量 HDF5_ROOT 指向 HDF5 安装的基础目录。之后重新运行 CMake 配置过程，它应该能够正确识别头文件位置。 #### 示例代码片段 以下是完整的 CMakeLists.txt 片段示例，展示如何链接 HDF5 和指定其头文件路径： cmake find_package(HDF5 REQUIRED COMPONENTS CXX) if(NOT HDF5_FOUND) message(FATAL_ERROR "HDF5 not found!") endif() message(STATUS "Using HDF5 include directories: ${HDF5_INCLUDE_DIRS}") add_executable(hdf5_test main.cpp) target_include_directories(hdf5_test PRIVATE ${HDF5_INCLUDE_DIRS}) target_link_libraries(hdf5_test PRIVATE ${HDF5_CXX_LIBRARIES} ${HDF5_LIBRARIES}) #### 注意事项 - 确保已正确安装 HDF5 开发包。对于基于 Debian 的系统，这通常是通过 apt-get install libhdf5-dev 实现。 - 若遇到编译错误提示找不到 hdf5.h 文件，则可能是由于未正确传递头文件路径给编译器所致[^2]。 ---

The change was ... someone can take the apk created when AS ... a release build and upload it directly ... the play store.
...
We have debug, release and distribute builtTypes. Debug is just for debugging, release is for testing (it has enabled logs and debug symbols, but contains native code optimization and uses ProGuard (on Java)), and distribute is builtType from which production APK is built (it has same optimization level as release, but with debug logs and debug symbols turned off).
...
build our production APKs from terminal by directly invoking gradle wrapper. ... option in Android Studio to ... in release/distribute buildType ... when you click run, ... dialog asking you to select device on which you want to run pops out and you ... safely build only ABI for selected device ... when you click Build ... Generate Signed APK, you want to build signed APK that will be uploaded to PlayStore
...
way, we do infer it from user action. If you click Build->>Generate Signed APK, Android Studio does create libraries for all ABI.
The current issue is that we are not differentiating between whether the aar produced by the library plugin was for a debug or release apk. The plan is to have Android Studio pass this information to Gradle, so that if you are building for a debuggable apk, Gradle will build for only a single ABI even when it is building the release variant of the library.
...
Our concern is that this would lead to creation of release variant apks that are (silently) missing some/most ABIs but that can be uploaded to the Play store without getting a warning. It would be pretty bad both for developers and for Play users if someone did that by accident. By requiring the debug flag, we ensure that the apk generates a warning when it's uploaded to Play and hopefully prevent that issue.
...
On the other hand, if you are concerned that some people might use 3rd party plugins which automatically upload release build APKs to Play Store may have problems with such a configuration, then a good option would be to add a setting in build types section in build.gradle which would define for each build type whether or ... to build this build type ... for active architecture (this same trick ... Xcode for iOS ... enabled by default for debug builds and disabled for release builds and you can create your own build types (just like in gradle) and for each build type configure whether or not only active architecture or all architectures are being built (active architecture denotes the architecture of device on which app will be run)).
...
We put it behind a flag now. If you want to build only the ABI for the device, you can set android.buildOnlyTargetAbi=true in the gradle.properties files, or pass -Pandroid.buildOnlyTargetAbi=true to the gradle command.

fixed in 2.4
